summary: Defines the basic principle of establishing a mesh in which interoperating directory services exchange index objects, using the Common Indexing Protocol. It reports results from the TISDAG project.

eli5.summary: Phone books can share short indexes with each other so a search can find which book has the answer.

subtitle: Building networks of interconnected directory gateways that share index objects.

tldr.problem: A single centralized directory gateway may not scale to serve entire regions, and different countries or organizations may each want their own gateway while still allowing searches across boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: Multiple DAG servers can form a mesh by exchanging index objects using the Common Indexing Protocol (CIP). Each DAG server aggregates the index objects from its local providers and shares them with other DAG servers, allowing queries to be routed across the network.
tldr.outcome: Users can search from any DAG server and receive referrals to services in other geographic or organizational regions, enabling distributed load-sharing and federated directory services.

facts.label: Mesh coordination mechanism
facts.value: Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) index object exchange

facts.label: Supported interoperability scenarios

today: RFC 2968 is Informational and documents the TISDAG project's experience with mesh architectures as of October 2000. The document acknowledges several open questions about mesh deployment that remained theoretical at the time.

sections.title: From Single Gateway to Mesh
sections.content:
The basic TISDAG architecture (see RFC 2967) creates a single referral gateway that collects indexes from many whitepages providers within one region or country. The obvious next step is to extend that design beyond a single gateway.

This RFC explores how multiple DAG servers can interconnect to form a mesh. The key principle is that interoperating services should exchange index objects according to the mesh architecture—whether that is hierarchical (with a top-level server and subordinate servers) or a flat peer-to-peer network. Meshes avoid simply forwarding provider index objects unchanged; instead, each DAG server aggregates the indexes from its local providers and shares aggregated summaries with other DAG servers.

This separation serves an important purpose: individual services may support different access protocols, have particular security requirements, or use different schemas, so referrals should direct queries to recognized gateways (and their access points), not directly to individual providers.
sections.eli5: Instead of one big phone book system, many smaller systems can work together. Each system keeps its own list of books, and they share those lists with each other so searches can go anywhere.

sections.title: Mesh Scenarios and Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC outlines three main scenarios. In Case 1, two countries running identical DAG systems can connect by having each country's DAG serve as a WDSP to the other country's system. A query in Country A that matches data indexed from Country B's service generates a referral back to Country B's system. If the client protocol supports referrals (Whois++ or LDAPv3), the client can follow the referral directly; otherwise, Country A's CAP can chain the query through one of Country A's SAPs to reach Country B.

In Case 2, the two countries use different protocols or schemas. Country A can establish a special SAP that translates between Country A's semantics and Country B's service, allowing meaningful queries to cross the boundary even though the services differ internally. Alternatively, Country B can establish a CAP specifically designed to receive queries from Country A, handling all the translation.

Case 3 applies when the two systems are so similar that direct WDSP index copying and SAP-to-SAP connections become practical, reducing the overhead of aggregation and aggregation reversal.
sections.eli5: Three ways to connect: same-system meshes can just pass queries through; different systems need translators between them; and very compatible systems can connect their pieces directly.

sections.title: Mesh Topology and Future Work
sections.content:
The RFC describes two complementary strategies for expanding queries in a mesh. In the top-down model, a query at a lower-level server may be expanded upward to a higher-level server that can search across multiple geographic regions. In the bottom-up model, queries can be expanded by discovering which other servers in the mesh have relevant indexes and are willing to participate.

The DAG/IP protocol includes control constructs (such as the polled-by system command) to allow CAPs to discover the mesh topology and decide whether to broaden query scope. However, the RFC acknowledges that experience with real server meshes was limited at the time of writing, and several questions remained open: should scope expansion always happen, happen only on user request, or happen based on local referral availability? Should expansion use a local SAP or direct CAP-to-CAP connections? Should meshes be completely connected or more hierarchical?

The RFC also notes that individual WDSPs may wish to restrict whether their data can be included in aggregated index objects sent to other mesh participants, allowing selective participation in the broader federation.
sections.eli5: Queries can flow up and down the network based on what information is where. Different mesh designs (hierarchical or fully connected) might work better in different situations.

sections.title: Implications for Federated Services
sections.content:
The mesh architecture described in this RFC shows how the TISDAG concept can scale beyond a single national gateway. By allowing DAG servers to aggregate and share index objects using CIP, multiple independent services can participate in a larger federation while maintaining their autonomy and local control.

This approach addresses the practical reality that different regions, countries, or organizations may want to operate their own directory gateway but still allow their users to search across boundaries. The key insight is that the same protocol-mapping efficiency and schema-translation mechanisms that allow TISDAG to bridge different client protocols and backends can also bridge different geographic DAG services.
sections.eli5: Multiple directory systems can work together as a federated network without any of them losing control over their own data or operations.

viz.caption: Two approaches to connecting DAG services

left.title: Pass-through mesh
left.desc: Identical services exchange indexes and clients can follow referrals directly or CAPs chain queries.

right.title: Translation mesh
right.desc: Different services use translating SAPs or CAPs to map between different protocols and schemas.
